abstract: The macaque Superior Temporal Sulcus (STS) is a brain area that receives and integrates inputs from both the ventral and dorsal visual processing streams (thought to specialize in form and motion processing respectively). For the processing of articulated actions, prior work has shown that even a small population of STS neurons contains sufficient information for the decoding of actor invariant to action, action invariant to actor, as well as the specific conjunction of actor and action. This paper addresses two questions. First, what are the invariance properties of individual neural representations (rather than the population representation) in STS? Second, what are the neural encoding mechanisms that can produce such individual neural representations from streams of pixel images? We find that a baseline model, one that simply computes a linear weighted sum of ventral and dorsal responses to short action “snippets”, produces surprisingly good fits to the neural data. Interestingly, even using inputs from a single stream, both actor-invariance and action-invariance can be produced simply by having different linear weights.

summary.idea: A simple model combines responses to short action fragments from visual pathways associated with form and motion. Different linear weights produce different kinds of selectivity.
summary.limitations: A successful fit does not by itself establish the brain's causal mechanism. The abstract does not report dataset size, quantitative fit quality, or performance beyond the measured action stimuli.
summary.problem: Some brain responses distinguish an action despite changes in its actor, while others distinguish the actor across actions. Explaining these individual-neuron responses from visual input remains challenging.
summary.results: The model fits the recorded neural responses surprisingly well. Even a single input pathway can support actor-invariant or action-invariant responses through different weighting patterns.
summary.tldr: Simple weighted combinations of short visual action fragments can explain several observed forms of neural invariance.

title: Neural representation of action sequences: how far can a simple snippet-matching model take us?
